learning: Container bone holds every bone except the shadow; the shadow has its own 2 bones and 1 mesh outside it, so it can scale down on jumps.
Under body, two rotation-only sibling bones (hip and chest) give the spine its curve and a second layer of motion. Cow: spine_back>hips and spine_front>chest.
The body mesh binds to the red controller bones, not the IK children, so manual motion can still be layered on top.
Tail is a 2-5 bone chain drawn with the Pose tool; the tip is weighted 100% to one bone so it does not deform.
Legs use 2-bone IK with Stretch on; the target is a child of the paw bone, so the paw is also the controller. Bone lengths in the pair are kept similar.
Rear legs get an extra hand-moved 'reversed bone' instead of a second IK. It keeps the foot planted, adds lean, and scales for perspective.
With single IK, the targets stay on the ground when the body jumps. A transform constraint makes the target follow the leg while airborne.
Rear-leg IK targets are built from the root outward, outside the leg chain, so they are pure targets.
Foreground legs get the full rig. Background legs are simplified, or copied from the foreground set for consistency, and slot order decides which side reads in front.
Place the chest bone midway between the two front-leg chains so both shoulders rotate evenly.
No neck bone: 'if I need that neck animation I move the head bone'.
Ears are chains of at most 3 bones; scaling and skewing those bones gives volume. Ears follow the head through transform constraints, so the near ear goes back as the head moves.
A reverse bone behind the head, mirrored by a transform constraint at translate -100, carries hair and back volume for parallax.
Eyelid bones only bend the lid into a happy or sad curve. The blink is an attachment swap between closed and happy-closed, hidden by animating the lid bone first.
Separate eyes, upper and lower lids, lashes, pupils, nostrils and the mouth with its chin. Eyebrows stay in the head mesh but sit inside edge rings so they don't stretch the face.
Animal head rig: head > back_head, cheek_L/R, ear_L>ear_L1, ear_R>ear_R1, eyebrows, eye_L (ball, eyelid_closed, shine, IK ball chain), whiskers (1 bone each).
Vertices are dense only where a leg bends, and long thin triangles are avoided because they make 'bad deformation lines' when the leg rotates.
Paint one bone at a time with the others locked, then test the weights by posing in animation mode and reverting.
Colour controllers red. Put IK targets and rarely used bones in a named bone selection and hide them with its dot; don't make them transparent, because the next animator won't find them.
Keep images inside bones rather than the root folder, so ghosting and onion skin show the container.

Jump: animate only the main bone's Y, then rotation. Offset the body bones by 2 frames and hold the apex longer than physics allows. The face (emotion) comes before the legs, and tail, ears and fur come last.
When the body rises, translate the legs back to keep balance. Front legs lift first and land first, with front and back offset by 1 frame on landing.
A rabbit delivery has idle, idle_variation1-3, jump, eating, drinking, dance and wake animations, all on one rig.
Never animate root. The first bone is a 'character' container, which gets animated for jumps and exaggeration.
Pelvis is the first child of the container: Ctrl+click on the hip image puts the bone at the image centre. Then hip > leg > foot, and up the spine waist > chest > head.
Put the pivot in the middle of the round joint piece. A lower pivot gives better ground contact but a stranger bend.
No neck bone: the neck is a mesh whose top binds to head and bottom to chest.
Use as few bones as possible, because each one takes time to animate. One bone for a hair mass, one 3-bone finger with the rest faked, a single face bone.
Extra pivots under pelvis (pelvis2/3/5/7) and a chest2 helper split one body region into separately rotatable layers, for example the shoulder carrying a scar.
A big yellow helper bone with a custom icon, lightly weighted to waist and chest, bends the whole torso in one move.
A 'face' bone under head holds every face slot, and the face mesh is weighted to it. Scaling it fakes a 3D head turn. 'It took me 20 seconds.'
Turn off Inherit Rotation on shoulders, head and straps so they stay upright when the torso rotates. Turn off Inherit Scale on shoulders and neck so breathing scales only the chest.
Mesh only parts that bend (legs, hips, arms, torso, cloth, shadow). Props, eyes and highlights stay rigid region attachments parented to a bone.
A leg mesh can be 5 vertices dragged out from the bone origin: 'maybe this was totally enough... why complicate things?'
Away from a joint a vertex is 100% on one bone, with only a narrow blend band at the joint. The heel belongs to the foot bone (around 62/38 at the heel).
Keep triangles from crossing a detail you want intact (the scar), and bind that region 100% to one bone.
Finger mesh: 3 vertices on the outer edge of each bend and 2 on the inner edge give rigid phalanges.
Leg IK with Stretch: redraw the foot bone so it touches the shin end, or stretching slides it. A transform constraint (target-to-foot) lets one control bone both move and rotate the foot.
Don't IK an arm just to steer it with one bone, because you lose the forearm's follow-through. Use IK only for external contact: ground, table, wall, a two-handed weapon, a hand on the waist.
Bend the legs slightly before creating the IK, otherwise the knees have no bend direction and flip.
Knee controller: a 1-bone IK per leg bone (the mesh-bound set) plus a duplicate 2-bone IK chain on the same target, joined by a translate transform constraint, with the IK mix slightly under 100.
Talking mouth on a large character: lips and teeth are separate meshes bound to a container bone plus a scale bone locked at 30%, with a chin bone for the jaw. The mouth states are attachment swaps.
For small characters, 3 swapped mouth states (idle, open1, open2) are enough. Keep the closed state close to idle.
Idle base: a 60-frame breathing loop on a chest-expansion bone, then separate rotation timelines on the arms with offsets, 'not noticeable, but not static'.

Duplicate the base idle and add a weight shift, step, face turn or mouth swap. Key everything at both transition edges (Ctrl+Shift+L) so the segments outside stay untouched, and move the hip 8 frames before the foot.
'Everything moves in a curved path': split the hip's X and Y timelines and offset them.
Bring the rig to 80% and start animating. The rig keeps changing until the final stages.
The pelvis sits a little behind the body so the main movement rotates believably. The foot IK targets are the ball bones, moved under the container, which saves two bones.
One full 3-bone finger chain; the other fingers are faked. The face is 2 face pieces plus the head, with no constraints.
One slot holds two leg attachments (a standing leg and a contact-correct leg), swapped by key.
Don't cut limbs into pieces you don't need: a cloth arm bends fine as one mesh. Where you must cut, end the pieces round.
Deliver a straightened copy of curved parts (hair, tail, cloth) using Puppet Warp or Liquify, so bones lie along a straight shape.
Realistic anthro head: a face_3D bone under chest7 drives all face parts, and the 3-bone ear chains carry the long ears.
Face weight falloff: 100% at the centre or tip, about 80% at the nose, down to 0-5% at the ears. Move, scale and shear on that one bone give fake 3D.
Hero-size faces only: container bones skewed into a ring (ear, cheekbone, nose) orbit when the control bone rotates. It takes about an hour, so 'mostly I don't do this'.
Wing: elbow and wrist joint bones are siblings under the shoulder (added with Shift), and each joint has a red manual control bone.
A short IK at the tip plus transform constraints at 50% mix make the middle bones follow the controller halfway. Use Recalculate Order when constraints fight.
Spine 4.3: one IK plus three additive, clamped transform constraints turn the hip's X into a procedural step. A narrow source range mapped to a wide target range gives speed.
Long body mesh: manual (orange) edges run across the body at each bone, and bones sit on vertex rows so it bends cleanly.
Horse- or spider-type legs: reverse the foot bone and put the IK target inside it.
Plan the animation before cutting. Cut only the pieces the animation needs ('without really understanding what the animation is going to be' is the mistake).
Symbols with the same shape share one rig and differ only by skin. The same layer name across skins makes one slot, and tints go on the attachment colour, not the slot colour.
Flat props such as a shield get shear plus scale for a 3D turn, with no mesh or constraint.
Photoshop-to-Spine script tags. Groups: [bone], [slot], [skin], [merge], [folder], [ignore]. Layers: [ignore], [path:name]. The ruler origin becomes 0,0 in Spine.

Native PSD import (Spine 4.2+/4.3) adds [mesh], [mesh:source] (a linked mesh), [skin:name], [overlay] (a clipping mask), [origin] (layer centre = root) and a rotation tag. The PSD stays linked and refreshes on re-import.
Layer name = attachment name = bone name, and names must be unique or the export fails. Part pivots are not set in the PSD; the animator places them in Spine.
Re-import doesn't convert existing region attachments to meshes. Delete them and import again, and expect to re-mesh and re-weight a new skin.

Hold Alt with the Create tool and draw over a bone to redraw its position and rotation; children and attachments stay. To find a pivot, loop between two extreme poses and Alt-tap until the bend looks right.

Weight Smooth spreads only along edges. Orange manual edges are the routes it follows. They also control triangulation, select whole rings (Shift-click), and close a loop so you can delete part of a mesh.
Prune (max bones per vertex plus a threshold) helps performance but hurts smoothness. Smooth once or twice on selected vertices only.
Avoid deform keys as patches: a mesh gets one timeline, the vertices travel in straight lines, and keying 5 deforms on every mesh more than doubled the JSON. Add bones and weights instead.

IK is limited to 1 or 2 bones, and the target can never be a child of the chain. It needs inherit rotation and scale on. Softness > 0 disables stretch, and Bend Positive can only be keyed while the chain is straight.

Slider (4.3): make one key per pose in an animation, Create Slider, then pick a controller bone and its rotation (world space). Rotating that bone scrubs the poses. Disable the slider while editing the poses.
Before rigging, ask the developers which Spine version they run and whether meshes and constraints are allowed.
Resize the art to the target resolution before import so bones don't have to be scaled up.
Animal eyes are built in empty sockets. The head is painted with skin under the eyes, and the eye sits on top as stacked parts: ball, closed lid, lid, shine, pupil.
Pupils sit at the end of a short bone chain (pup_r2 > r3 > r4 > r6) aimed by one shared `target` bone, so moving that one bone points both eyes. The eyelid is a mesh that follows.
An orange elbow helper bone sits at the sleeve fold so the sleeve bends round instead of creasing.
The hand that grips the cane has a hand base with f1–f5 finger bones and a left-arm IK, because the hand touches an external object (consistent with the IK-only-for-contact rule).
Crab-like creature: each leg is a 2-bone IK chain with its own target. Animations: attack, attack_skill, breathe, levelup, prone, special1, walk.
Realistic creature face: upper and lower lids each have idle and closed attachments plus lid bones; separate eyebrow bones; red mouth-corner bones.
The upper lip curve is a path constraint ('top-lip'). A row of head bones rides the path and the lip mesh is weighted to them, so bending the path moves the whole lip smoothly.
Large wing: each feather row is its own bone chain inside the wing mesh, with orange control bones at the joints.
Semi-realistic quadruped: dozens of small fur and mane bones (bone56–bone90), plus nose, beard and mouth bones, for secondary motion on a furry silhouette.
Hanging lantern: each rope is a multi-bone chain with a control bone at its end.
Book page: a regular grid mesh weighted to many page bones, so the page can curl during a flip.
Owl tail feathers splay through 2-bone IK with high softness (≈148), Positive bend and stretch off. Softness is used here, unlike on legs.
The body and the outfit are separate skin groups (Character/old, young × Outfits/outfit-old, young), combined at runtime. The skirt mesh is weighted to the front-leg bones.
A curved collar is one mesh weighted along a chain of about 9 collar bones that follows the curve, so it deforms with the shoulders.
Digitigrade legs (animal-shaped legs on a biped) are a 3-bone chain plus foot, with an IK target at the toe.
Held staff: hand_L is a child of the staff bone and arm_IK targets that hand, so animating the staff drags the arm along. A VFX_Container bone holds the effects.
A belt pouch gets its own 3 bones and a weighted mesh for secondary jiggle. The rig grew from 44 to 57 bones during the session.
Front-view rig: each arm slot holds front and three-quarter-view hand attachments, swapped per pose. The trouser legs have in-front and behind-leg slots for layering during the walk.
Frontal walk rig starts from a symmetric arms-out pose, with straight single bones per leg segment.

Background from one flat painting: select each element (Color Range for foliage, selection for the wheel), move it to its own layer, then paint or clone the area it covered so the layer below is complete.
After cutting the wheel out, the ground behind it is repainted, so moving the wheel never reveals a hole.
In Spine, the clouds ride a path constraint across the scene.
Painterly art is cut with Select and Mask (refined, soft edge), not a hard lasso, so the cut part keeps its brush texture.
Hidden areas are rebuilt with the Clone Stamp, sampling nearby texture, on the layer behind the cut element.
Flat image to rig-ready: the arms come off as their own layers and the torso is repainted complete underneath them, including the parts the arms covered.
Layer groups follow the body: Head, Body (Neck, M Body, R Arm, L Arm), Lower Body, Back Hair, Wing. The groups later become bones or deformers.
Eye layer stack, per side: white, pupil (iris), highlight, lower lash, upper lash (eyelash), eyelid, plus a separate eyebrow, named L/R.
Long hair tails are split into segments A, B, C plus the hair-tie piece, so each segment can bend.
Underfill: a flat, darker copy of a part's silhouette sits under it, so a gap that opens while moving reads as shadow, not as a hole.
The face separates into skin, underfill, an outline ring (face line), blush, blush marks and a front-hair shadow, each its own layer.
A sleeve separates into the sleeve, top and bottom fills, ribbons, a pocket, and an underfill for each, so its folds can move independently.
Back hair is painted as a complete shape under the front hair and face, not only the visible strands.
The mouth is split into lips, teeth, tongue and an interior painted as its own shapes (the 'standard method'). The quick 'simple method' leaves eyes and mouth less separated.
Joint caps: draw a circle centred on each pivot (hip, knee, elbow) and merge it into the limb end, so the overlap stays round when the limb rotates.
Upper arm and forearm both end in round caps that overlap at the elbow.

Prep sheet: front, three-quarter, side and back views, plus straightened copies of the tail and pigtails. PhotoshopToSpine v7.24 settings: ignore hidden layers, ignore background layer, trim whitespace, scale 100%, padding 1.
Each part gets its own outline (a stroke layer style) so separated pieces keep a line where they overlap.
